question: `const AuthContext = createContext({ user: null, login: () => {} })`. A login button rendered outside the provider is clicked. What happens?
options: Nothing visible: the default no-op `login` runs silently
The button logs the user in through the nearest provider
explanation: Default values are used when no provider exists, so the bug is hidden. A `null` default plus a guarded hook that throws makes the misplacement obvious.

question: A team needs: (a) the current locale for the whole app, (b) a cursor position updated 60 times per second and read by 40 components, (c) the open step of a wizard used inside that wizard. Which are good fits for context?
explanation: Context is ideal for rarely changing app-wide values and for feature-scoped state. High-frequency state read by many components re-renders every consumer on each change; an external store with selectors fits (b).

question: A provider renders `<Ctx value={{ items, add }}>`. Its parent re-renders because of an unrelated clock. What happens to `memo` consumers of `Ctx`?
options: They all re-render, because the value is a new object on every provider render
React warns and skips the update
explanation: Context compares the value with `Object.is`. An inline object is new each time. `useMemo` for the object and `useCallback` for the functions keep it stable.

question: Which is a valid use of `use(ThemeContext)` that `useContext` does not allow?
options: Reading the context inside a class component
Reading the context inside an `if` block in a component
Reading a context without any provider
explanation: `use` can be called conditionally and in loops (it is not bound to the order of Hooks). It still only reads the nearest provider's value.

question: A dashboard renders three independent chart widgets, each with its own "selected series" state shared by the widget's legend and plot. What is the cleanest design?
options: A `ChartProvider` around each widget, so each instance has its own scoped state
One context at the root holding all three selections
explanation: Each provider element creates an independent instance of its state for its subtree. Scoping per widget avoids ids, global coupling and cross-widget re-renders.
